title: Cheap lessons, self-taught players and Emil Williams's Rhapsody in Blue
summary: Goodwin compares lesson costs then and now and praises self-taught Emil Williams, who played Rhapsody in Blue from the score.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: I notice I run across fellows that can't read, you know, some guys playing rock and roll or country western or what have you, you know, but you find more people I think reading music and I think their opportunities are greater and when I was coming along, well I think you could take lessons for $.50, you know. The same lessons you pay $5.00 for now for half an hour. They were $.50 and you'd get a whole hour and well you couldn't find the $.50.

If you were poor, you know, you just had to do the best you could. There are so many self-taught musicians that came along then. One of the greatest ones I think -- we've mentioned him several times; Emil Williams. He was more or less a self-taught musician and he could take songs like "Rhapsody in Blue" and all those big, heavy numbers. I think "Rhapsody in Blue" had about 32 pages and I was working with him, just the, with just the two of us. I was singing and playing the guitar and he was playing piano and he went to town and bought Rhapsody in Blue and don't you know I've never heard it rendered more beautifully.
He would never play it on a job, not 32 pages because that would take the night but he would just play different -- maybe a couple of pages, a couple of movements tonight,

you know, just to let the people hear, you know, that 'Yeah, I'm not just sitting here. My ear is not the only thing that's working. My fingers and my brain works too'. Bring out the point that, 'I do read music'.
